Who sets and collects property tax

The county does the work here. It sets the tax on land, buildings and mobile homes, collects it, and splits the money among itself, cities, townships, school districts and other local districts. The State Tax Commissioner publishes the calendar and oversees the state boards, yet your check goes to the county treasurer.

Your bill comes from multiplying taxable value by the mill rate each taxing entity levies. Values are set as of February 1. Assessed value is half of market value, 50 percent of what the house would fetch on an open sale. The county auditor builds the tax list and delivers it to the treasurer by December 10, and the treasurer must mail a statement by December 26.

Selling? Phone the treasurer early. Ask what the parcel currently owes and whether a prior year is unsettled.

Due dates and penalties

Real estate tax is due on January 1 following the year it was levied and becomes delinquent after March 1 for a single payment or the first installment. Under N.D.C.C. 57-20-01, a first installment still unpaid after March 1 is charged 3 percent, and 3 percent more on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment becomes delinquent after October 15 and takes a 6 percent penalty.

DateWhat happens
January 1Tax for the prior levy year is due
February 15Pay the whole year's tax by this date for a 5 percent discount
March 1First installment is penalty-free through this day
October 15Second installment is penalty-free through this day
November 1Abatement applications for the earlier year's tax are due
December 26Treasurers mail the new tax statements

If a due date falls on a day the treasurer's office is closed, payment on the next open day carries no penalty and no loss of discount. A statement that never arrives is not an excuse. Failure to receive one does not relieve the owner or extend the February 15 discount deadline.

The 5 percent early-payment discount

The county treasurer allows a 5 percent discount to taxpayers who pay all of a parcel's real estate tax for the year on or before February 15. It applies to general taxes for the state, county, city, township, school district and other districts. It does not apply to special assessment installments, and it is figured before the Primary Residence Credit.

  • A county commission can extend the discount period by 30 days if it finds a weather or other emergency.
  • Installments must be at least 10 percent of the tax and never less than $10.
  • No discount applies to payment on property that has delinquent tax.

Money paid on a parcel with older tax owed goes first to the oldest delinquent amount, along with its penalty and interest. A seller catching up before closing should expect the payment to be applied that way.

How to appeal your assessment

An owner can appeal through a chain of equalization boards that meet in a fixed order during spring and summer. The assessor must deliver written notice of the value at least 15 days before the local board meets, and the notice gives the dates of the local and county board meetings.

  • Township and city boards of equalization sit in April on locally chosen dates. Ask the county or city auditor for yours.
  • The county board sits within the first 10 days of June. Owners may appear personally, send a representative, or appeal by mail stating their reasons.
  • The State Board of Equalization takes up locally assessed property on the second Tuesday in August. Individuals can speak and submit written material or photographs. The Property Tax division takes questions at propertytax@nd.gov or 701-328-3127.

If you disagree with a bill after it is issued, two more routes exist. You can pay under protest to the county treasurer with written reasons, then apply to the county commissioners within 60 days for abatement, adjustment or a refund. The separate abatement application for an earlier year's tax is due by November 1.

Credits that lower a homeowner's bill

Three state credits can reduce what a homeowner owes. The Primary Residence Credit is up to $1,600 against the tax due, for an owner who lives in a house, mobile home, town home, duplex or condo as a primary residence, with no age or income limits. A homeowner can also hold the Homestead or Disabled Veteran's credit and still use the Primary Residence Credit on any remaining balance.

  • Primary Residence Credit: up to $1,600, never more than the tax due. You must live there. The window opens in January and closes April 1.
  • Homestead Property Tax Credit: meant for owners who are 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, and whose income the year before the assessment date was $70,000 or less.
  • Disabled Veteran's Property Tax Credit: lowers taxable value by as much as $9,000 for a 100 percent rating, and the owner can carry it to a new homestead.

A credit stays with the resident, not the house. The next owner applies on their own after moving in.

When property tax goes unpaid

An unpaid balance becomes a lien on the property. Once two years or more have gone by, the county may foreclose and take title by tax deed. Each year from November 1 to 15 the treasurer mails every delinquent owner a notice saying the tax is a lien, and that foreclosure will follow unless it is paid by October 1 of the second year after delinquency.

The auditor must give foreclosure notice by June 1. The foreclosure date is October 1 after service, and the tax deed then passes the property to the county free of most encumbrances. Section 57-28-04 adds foreclosure costs of $50 or actual costs, whichever is higher, to the amount needed to clear the lien. A residential property gets personal service by the sheriff if the owner lives in the state.

Tax deed land is appraised, then sold at auction starting the third Tuesday in November for cash or one-fourth down with the balance over up to ten years. Buying the property back is possible for the former owner, the owner's executor, or a parent, spouse or child, but only before the county sells. A surplus over the taxes and costs is held 90 days for the record owner.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company subtracts what is owed, penalty and interest included, from the seller's check. The treasurer then posts it against the oldest year. The title company checks the treasurer's records for current and delinquent tax and for special assessments, which are billed with the tax.

Steps worth taking before you list:

  • Have the county treasurer quote you a payoff number ahead of closing day.
  • Check the first and second installment status for the year, since the second is not delinquent until after October 15.
  • Ask whether any special assessment installments are outstanding.
  • For an inherited house, find out who got the tax statement, since only one owner at the last-known address receives it.

A practical order of events: order the payoff figure, review the title company's search for liens and special assessments, confirm the treasurer has your correct mailing address, and sign the closing statement only after the tax line matches the payoff letter. Sellers who inherited a house often find an old year still open, and that is far easier to fix before a buyer is waiting than on closing day.

Who bears this year's tax, you or the buyer, is spelled out in the purchase contract. Check that clause with your agent or attorney. If a lien notice has already been mailed, speed matters, because the October 1 foreclosure date is fixed by statute. With a cash sale nobody waits on a mortgage approval, so payoff can follow signing quickly. Once the overdue amount is paid out of your proceeds, the county's claim on the house ends.

Frequently asked questions

What is the North Dakota property tax due date?

Payment is due January 1, and the tax turns delinquent once March 1 passes. You may split it into two installments, the second penalty-free through October 15. Pay it all by February 15 and the bill drops 5 percent.

What penalty applies to late North Dakota property tax?

A first installment paid late costs 3 percent after March 1, plus 3 percent at each of May 1, July 1 and October 15. A late second installment gets 6 percent after October 15.

How do I appeal my North Dakota property assessment?

Go first to the township or city board in April, next to the county board in early June, then to the State Board in August. The value notice is due to you at least 15 days before the local board sits.

How much is the North Dakota Primary Residence Credit?

It takes up to $1,600 off the tax due. Age and income do not matter. You need to live in the home and file by April 1.

Can I sell if I still owe property tax in North Dakota?

Yes. At closing the balance is deducted from what you receive, oldest year first. Closing before the foreclosure date also keeps the county from taking the house by tax deed.
